desc:
There are piles of candies, piles[i] in pile i. You may split any pile into as many smaller piles as you like, but you may never merge candies from different piles. Then you hand out the resulting piles to k children so that every child gets exactly one pile and all children get the same number of candies (some piles can stay unused).

Return the largest number of candies each child can receive, or 0 if even one candy per child is impossible.

Example: piles = [5, 8, 6], k = 3. Everyone can get 5 candies (5 from the first pile, 5 from the second, 5 from the third), but 6 is impossible: the piles give only 0 + 1 + 1 = 2 portions of size 6. The answer is 5.
hints: Suppose every child must receive exactly c candies. How many children can one pile of size p serve?
It serves p // c children, so the whole row serves sum(p // c). This number does not increase when c grows.
Binary search c in [1, max(piles)] for the largest value with sum(p // c) ≥ k. If even c = 1 fails (the total number of candies is below k), return 0.
editorial: For a fixed portion size c the number of children that can be served is g(c) = sum(p // c); leftovers inside a pile are wasted because piles cannot be merged. As c increases, every term shrinks or stays, so g is non-increasing. The feasible portion sizes are therefore 1..c*, and we search for the last one.
Check g(1) = sum(piles) ≥ k first; if not, answer 0. Otherwise search between 1 and max(piles) with an upper-mid binary search. Time is O(n log max(piles)), space O(1).
